title: In my own words
subtitle: Between worlds · Wednesday, 7:05 PM
focus: You can choose what to share, and how to say it.

scenes.title: The version for home

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: By Wednesday, our project has a title: A Place at the Table. Mom agreed that we could record the sounds of preparing dinner, but asked us not to record her conversations.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: We used the kettle, the cupboard door, and the scrape of chairs on the floor. Jules recorded the walk back to campus. Minh edited the two places together.

lines.speaker: Mom
lines.text: Bài ở lớp thế nào rồi con?
lines.translation: How is your class project going?

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: We are clearing the table. I could give her the title, the assignment, the whole argument about recording an ordinary evening. Or I could start with the part she helped make.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: At school, I have been talking about language and belonging. Here, those words feel a little distant from the person handing me a wet plate.

scenes.prompt: What version do you share with Mom?

note.title: Changing the frame
note.text: Choosing details for an audience does not necessarily make an account dishonest. Each option here is true within the story. An can explain the academic frame, begin with a shared experience, or keep the answer short without being scored for closeness to family.

choices.label: Explain the project’s question about language and belonging.
choices.detail: Invite her into the ideas you discuss at school.
choices.reflection: You shared the academic frame. Mom connected the abstract question to her own experience.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Tụi con làm về ngôn ngữ và cảm giác thuộc về một nơi.”
reaction.translation: We're working on language and the feeling of belonging somewhere.

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Như lúc mẹ ở chỗ làm khác với lúc ở nhà à?
reaction.translation: Like how I am at work compared with how I am at home?

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I had been preparing to explain a difficult idea. Mom already has her own way into it. I ask what changes for her at work.

choices.label: Start with the kitchen sounds she helped you record.
choices.detail: Begin with something you both know.
choices.reflection: You began with a shared moment. Mom heard her own contribution before hearing the theory.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Có tiếng ấm nước nhà mình trong bài đó mẹ.”
reaction.translation: The sound of our kettle is in the project, Mom.

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Cái ấm kêu to quá đó hả? Vậy mà cũng có ích.
reaction.translation: That noisy kettle? So it turned out to be useful.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I play her the short clip. She recognizes the cupboard before I point it out. We talk about why a sound can make somewhere feel familiar.

choices.label: “It’s going well. Can I show you after we finish the dishes?”
choices.detail: Keep it brief and choose a better moment.
choices.reflection: You chose the timing of the conversation. A short answer did not have to close the subject.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Ổn mẹ. Rửa chén xong con cho mẹ nghe nhé?”
reaction.translation: It's going well. Can I play it for you after we finish the dishes?

reaction.speaker: Mom
reaction.text: Ừ. Lau cái đĩa này trước đi.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: There is relief in finishing one thing before starting another. I set my phone on the counter for later and reach for the towel.

scenes.title: The version for friends

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: Later, Jules calls to check the captions for our audio. One caption translates Mom's dinner question, which I recorded again in my own voice with her permission.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: Listening to this, you sound different in Vietnamese. Softer, maybe? Does it feel like being a different person?

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I know Jules is curious. I also know the recording is from a quiet kitchen, and most of our English conversations happen while rushing between classes.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: There is something interesting in the question, but I do not want to become a demonstration of what every bilingual person is like.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: You don't have to answer that for the project. I'm asking you, not the microphone.

scenes.prompt: How much do you want to unpack?

note.title: A person, not a representative
note.text: An's response describes An, not all bilingual people. Language, audience, setting, mood, and relationships can overlap. None of these choices identifies a more authentic self, and choosing privacy is not a failed conversation.

choices.label: “Still me. You’re also hearing me in a different situation.”
choices.detail: Question the assumption without shutting down curiosity.
choices.reflection: You separated the sound of a language from the setting in which Jules heard it.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: True. You also sound different when we are presenting versus complaining about the printer.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Exactly. Vietnamese matters to me, but so does talking to my mom instead of presenting to a room.”

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: I'll change the caption from “two sides of An” to “two places in An's day.” Tell me if that still feels off.

choices.label: “Some parts of me come forward more easily in each language.”
choices.detail: Share a feeling without making it a universal rule.
choices.reflection: You shared a personal difference while leaving room for other people's experiences.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Certain jokes come easily at home. Most of my school vocabulary comes in English. That is about where I use the words, too. Minh might answer differently.”

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: So I shouldn't turn your answer into a caption about all bilingual people.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Please don't.” I am glad they asked, and glad I got to put a boundary around the answer.

choices.label: “I’m not ready to put that into words tonight.”
choices.detail: Keep this part of your experience private.
choices.reflection: You set a boundary. Jules could respect it without needing a fuller explanation.

reaction.speaker: Jules
reaction.text: Okay. Thanks for telling me. We can just label the places and the speakers.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “That would be good.” We return to the captions. I do not feel less like their friend because I left one question unanswered.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: Before we hang up, Jules sends a photo of the recorder with a note: I finally learned which button to press. Some jokes need no translating now.

scenes.title: What the listener takes home

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: The next morning, we sit together for one last listen. A cupboard closes. Footsteps fade into campus noise. My voice asks the dinner question, followed by its English caption.

lines.speaker: Minh
lines.text: We have room for a final line from you, if you want one. Something to connect the places.

lines.speaker: Jules
lines.text: Or we can let the sounds finish. It doesn't need to explain your whole life.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I look at our notes. So many small choices: what to translate, what to explain, when to wait, who gets to speak. None of them turned the evening into a perfect exchange.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: But we ate together. We made something together. There is more room in the conversation than there was when Jules first stood in our doorway.

lines.speaker: An
lines.text: I do not need a sentence that solves being bilingual. I only need to decide how I want this particular story to end.

scenes.prompt: What do you leave with the listener?

note.title: An ending, not a score
note.text: These endings emphasize connection, personal agency, or listening. None is a best ending. Your journal records the choices you made and their tradeoffs, rather than calculating how well you performed a language or an identity.

choices.label: “Understanding is something we make together.”
choices.detail: End with the work of connection.
choices.reflection: You ended with shared responsibility: listeners and speakers both help an exchange take shape.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I record the line, then ask Minh and Jules to listen. “Does that sound like what we made?” They each suggest a tiny change to the pause before it.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: At home, Mom asks how the presentation went. I tell her Jules can now hear our kettle in almost any recording. She says we should probably replace it.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I laugh, and then I tell her the rest. There is time for the longer answer tonight.

choices.label: “Both languages are mine. So is the choice of what to share.”
choices.reflection: You ended with agency: you can belong in more than one language without making everything public.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: I record the line in one take. It sounds more definite than I feel on some days, but it is a sentence I want to keep.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: After class, someone asks whether we will publish the recordings. I say we will check with everyone involved. Finishing the assignment does not change what Mom agreed to share.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: On the walk home, I send her a message in Vietnamese and Jules a message in English. Both sound like me.

choices.label: Let the kitchen sounds have the last word.
choices.detail: End with space for the listener.
choices.reflection: You ended with listening. Some meaning can remain open without being missing.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: “Let's leave the chair scrape in.” Minh adjusts the ending. For a few seconds, no one fills the silence with an explanation.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: After the presentation, a classmate says the sound reminded them of their grandmother's apartment. It is not my memory, but the recording made space for theirs.

reaction.speaker: An
reaction.text: That evening, I pull out a chair at home. Mom looks up. I have not said anything yet, and already there is a place for me.
